conclusion.justification: The report concludes that there is insufficient high-quality scientific evidence to prove hypnosis independently aids smoking cessation, treating the overall evidence as inconclusive while noting it may offer minor support as an adjunctive therapy.
conclusion.label: hedged

report:
**Conclusion:**
High-quality scientific evidence does not clearly prove that hypnosis independently drives successful smoking cessation, supporting your skepticism. However, research suggests it may offer minor assistance to some individuals when combined with broader treatment plans.

**Key Evidence:**
* **Lack of Clear Superiority:** Systematic reviews, including Cochrane reviews evaluating hypnotherapy for smoking cessation, found insufficient evidence to prove that hypnosis is consistently more effective than other behavioral interventions or no treatment (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6568235).
* **Inconsistent Outcomes:** A comprehensive meta-analysis examining hypnosis interventions found that out of six reported effects from systematic reviews on smoking cessation, only two showed statistically significant benefits (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1330238/full).
* **Adjunctive Support:** Medical institutions such as the Mayo Clinic note that while hypnosis is not a guaranteed standalone fix, it may be effective as part of a larger, comprehensive treatment plan (https://www.mayoclinic.org/tests-procedures/hypnosis/about/pac-20394405). Furthermore, medical reviews emphasize that additional rigorous research is necessary to confirm its effectiveness (https://www.healthline.com/health/hypnosis-to-quit-smoking).
